coredata.dc:description: Chalcopyrite and layered magnesium bearing silicate minerals (such as serpentine) are prone to heterogeneous aggregation under alkaline and weak acid conditions, which changed the surface properties of chalcopyrite and reduced the floatability of chalcopyrite when conventional collector such as sodium butyl xanthate (SBX) was used. To enhance the collection of chalcopyrite in the presence of serpentine, novel nanospheres of poly styrene-butyl acrylate (St-Ba) were prepared and used as collector to improve the floatability of the chalcopyrite minerals. The micro-flotation tests showed that the St-Ba nanospheres could well eliminate the inhibition of serpentine on the chalcopyrite and greatly increase the chalcopyrite recovery. Compared with SBX, the St-Ba nanospheres enhanced the floatation recovery from 89% to 95% for the single chalcopyrite mineral, and from 42% to 84% for the mixed ores of chalcopyrite and serpentine. Adsorption tests, contact angle measurement, SEM observation and Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation revealed that the St-Ba nanospheres could be firmly adsorbed on the surface of chalcopyrite, which could not only increase the mineral hydrophobicity, but also act as a bridge between chalcopyrite particles and air bubbles to enhance the floatability of the chalcopyrite. The results of this work indicated that the organic nanospheres was an effective novel collector and could be used to solve the inhibitory effect of gangue mineral fines on target mineral flotation.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Chalcopyrite and layered magnesium bearing silicate minerals (such as serpentine) are prone to heterogeneous aggregation under alkaline and weak acid conditions, which changed the surface properties of chalcopyrite and reduced the floatability of chalcopyrite when conventional collector such as sodium butyl xanthate (SBX) was used. To enhance the collection of chalcopyrite in the presence of serpentine, novel nanospheres of poly styrene-butyl acrylate (St-Ba) were prepared and used as collector to improve the floatability of the chalcopyrite minerals. The micro-flotation tests showed that the St-Ba nanospheres could well eliminate the inhibition of serpentine on the chalcopyrite and greatly increase the chalcopyrite recovery. Compared with SBX, the St-Ba nanospheres enhanced the floatation recovery from 89% to 95% for the single chalcopyrite mineral, and from 42% to 84% for the mixed ores of chalcopyrite and serpentine. Adsorption tests, contact angle measurement, SEM observation and Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation revealed that the St-Ba nanospheres could be firmly adsorbed on the surface of chalcopyrite, which could not only increase the mineral hydrophobicity, but also act as a bridge between chalcopyrite particles and air bubbles to enhance the floatability of the chalcopyrite. The results of this work indicated that the organic nanospheres was an effective novel collector and could be used to solve the inhibitory effect of gangue mineral fines on target mineral flotation.

ce:section.ce:para: Chalcopyrite, as the main raw material of copper smelting, is a common copper mineral, which is formed in different environments such as hydrothermal and contact metasomatism [1]. Up to date, froth flotation has always been the main way to obtain the chalcopyrite concentrates. However, as the main gangue mineral in copper nickel sulfide ore (mainly composed of chalcopyrite and pentlandite), serpentine is easy to agglomerate with copper nickel sulfide ore, which seriously affects the floatability of chalcopyrite [2]. Feng et al. [3,4] reported that serpentine and copper nickel sulfide particles aggregated together due to their opposite electric charges, and the surface of sulfide ore particles was easily covered by argillaceous serpentine, which reduced the floatability of sulfide ore. At present, ultrasonic treatment, high-intensity conditioning, chemical treatment and other technologies are used to remove magnesium from magnesium silicate mineral. These methods are used to disperse the serpentine from the surface of chalcopyrite, and weaken the influence of serpentine on the floatability of chalcopyrite [5,6]. Feng et al. [3] and Bulatovic and Salter [7] reported that the fluid force field generated by high-intensity conditioning could peel off the serpentine adhered to the surface of sulfide ore, which could weaken the influence of serpentine on the floatability of sulfide ore and provide more sites for the collector to adsorb on the surface of sulfide ore. Moreover, the shedding amount of serpentine was increased with the increase of stirring time and stirring intensity. Some other studies showed that the influence of serpentine on the floatability of sulfide ore could be weakened by adding inhibitors or changing the dosing sequence of collectors and inhibitors, optimizing the process flow and chemical pretreatment, so as to improve the concentrate recovery [8–11].

In recent years, nanotechnology has been developed rapidly. Based on the unique characteristics of nanoparticles such as the high specific surface area, good adsorption ability and easy surface functionalization, etc., it has been introduced into the field of mineral processing [12]. For example, nanobubbles have been applied to float the fine coal, which effectively improve the collision probability of ordinary air bubble with fine coal. The application of nanobubbles can not only improve the floatation recovery, but also reduce the collector dosage [13–15]. In the flotation test of quartz particles, the effects of particle size, air flow rate, Reynolds number, bubble amount on the quartz flotation recovery were evaluated. It was found that the adhesion of ordinary bubbles on the mineral surface was enhanced by nanobubbles, which effectively improve the flotation recovery of quartz particles [16–19]. Recently, nanospheres as collectors have attracted much attention, which can be divided into two categories: one is natural hydrophobic minerals, such as hydrophobic nanometer talc; the other is synthetic nanospheres, such as polystyrene [20]. In order to select suitable nanospheres as mineral flotation collectors, many scholars have studied large-scale nanospheres library and summarized the necessary characteristics of nanospheres as collectors: (1) the nanospheres must be hydrophobic enough to adhere to the bubbles; (2) the nanospheres must be well dispersed in the flotation slurry; (3) the nanospheres can be selectively adsorbed on the surface of target minerals rather than gangue minerals [21]. Hajati et al. used talc nanoparticles as collectors for quartz [22]. It was found that the recovery of quartz was improved by increasing the stirring time and reducing the particle size of the talc powder. A polymeric nanoparticle was used as the collector to enhance the floatability of the glass bead and/or pentlandite by Yang et al. [23,24]. It was found that the glass transition temperature of nanoparticles had a great effect on the floatation behavior. In other words, the softer particles were more deformable and could have a larger contact area with the glass bead or pentlandite. So, the softer nanoparticles could more firmly adhere to the surfaces of the glass bead or pentlandite to enhance floatability of the minerals. According to the research of Dong et al. [25,26], the smaller and more hydrophobic nanoparticles are the most effective as flotation collectors. However, there is a hypothesis that nanosphere collectors larger than gangue particles contribute to the adhesion of target mineral particles to air bubbles [27].

In this paper, larger poly St-Ba nanospheres were prepared and applied as collectors to enhanced flotation of chalcopyrite in the presence of serpentine. Different from previous studies, the size of the St-Ba nanospheres is larger than that of the serpentine. Therefore, through the bridging effect of the St-Ba nanospheres, chalcopyrite mineral particles can adhere to the surface of bubbles and be floated. The significant influence of St-Ba nanospheres on the flotation behavior of chalcopyrite and serpentine was investigated via micro-flotation tests. The selective adsorption behavior of St-Ba nanospheres on different mineral surfaces was studied through contact angle measurement, adsorption quantity tests, FT-IR, SEM and MD simulation. On the basis of the above analyses, a possible flotation mechanism of St-Ba nanospheres enhancing the flotation efficiency of chalcopyrite in the presence of serpentine was proposed.

Styrene (Analytical grade), butyl acrylate (99%) and 2,2-Azobis (2-methylpropyl) dihydrochloride (AIBA, 97%) were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Epoxy resin and curing agent were purchased from Shanghai Truer Industrial Development Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). SBX (90%) obtained from Yantai Junbang mineral separation materials Co., Ltd (Shandong, China) was dissolved in acetone, filtered and recrystallized with petroleum ether for three times. The purified xanthate was stored in a vacuum dryer for practice use.

Natural mineral samples of chalcopyrite and serpentine were obtained from Hubei Province of China and Jiangsu Province of China. The mineral samples were crushed with a hammer, and then the high-grade minerals were selected. The selected chalcopyrite particles were ground to −38 µm by XPM-Φ120 × 3 agate grinder (Wuhan Exploration Machinery Factory, China) for subsequent tests. The selected serpentine particles were ground to −10 µm by XPM-Φ120 × 3 agate grinder and JM-5 stirring mill (Changsha Tencan Powder Technology Co., Ltd, China). XRD analysis of the minerals was performed with a DX-2700 X-Ray diffractometer (Dandong Fangyuan Instrument Co., Ltd, China). Chemical multi-element detection illustrates that the contents of Cu, Fe and S in chalcopyrite are 33.92 wt%, 30.02 wt% and 34.53 wt% respectively, and the contents of MgO and SiO2 in serpentine are 42.82 wt% and 42.95 wt%, respectively. The XRD analysis ( Fig. 1) and chemical multi-element detection indicate that the purity of chalcopyrite and serpentine is high and exceeds 95%.

The St-Ba nanospheres were prepared by emulsion polymerization and illustrated in Fig. 2. Briefly, deionized water (200 mL) was added into a three necked bottle (500 mL), and then purged with N2 under stirring for 30 min at 70 °C. 6.96 g of styrene and 4.04 g of butyl acrylate were put into the deionized water and stirred for 10 min to mix the reagent and water together. After that, AIBA (0.084 g) dissolved in deionized water (10 mL) was then added into the above mixture solution and kept at 70 °C for 23 h [24]. With styrene and butyl acrylate as monomers and 2,2-Azobis (2-methylpropyl) dihydrochloride as initiator, the growth of St-Ba nanospheres was realized through the processes of CC double bond breaking, C-chain growth and C-chain termination. The product was purified by dialysis for one week to remove the remaining regents and stored in a plastic bottle.

A 40 mL XFGC II flotation machine (Jilin Exploration Machinery Factory, China) was used for mineral flotation tests, and the impeller stirring speed was controlled at 1992 rpm. The prepared minerals (2.0 g) and deionized water (40 mL) were placed in the flotation cell and stirred for 3 min to make them fully dispersed. Subsequently, HCl or NaOH solutions was used to adjust the pH of pulp, the collector of St-Ba or SBX was added into the flotation cell and stirred for another 3 min. Then, the foaming agent of MIBC was added into the pulp and stirred for 2 min before aeration. The mineral froths were collected every 10 s, and the concentrates and tailings were collected after continuous bubbling for 3 min. The concentrates and tailings were dried and weighed to calculate the recovery. In the single mineral micro-flotation test, the recovery is equal to the yield. In the mixed ore micro-flotation test, the yield is also taken as the recovery because the gangue consumption is very small and the overall recovery is considered in this paper.

The wettability of mineral surface can be directly reflected by the contact angle of mineral surface. In order to study the surface wettability of the mineral before and after interacting with the medicament, the contact angle of mineral was measured by a DSA 100 contact angle measuring instrument analyzer (KRÜSS, Germany). The mineral was fixed in an epoxy mold and cut to the appropriate size with a metallographic cutting machine (Unitom, Struers, USA). Then, the solidified samples were polished by tegramin-25 automatic grinding and polishing machine (Struers, USA) to expose a clean and fresh mineral surface. The polished mineral was immersed in a certain concentration of medicament solution for 5 min, washed with deionized water and dried. Finally, the contact angle of mineral treated by chemical reagents was determined.

The aggregation/dispersion of mineral particles was evaluated by measuring the turbidity of the mixture solution with a WZS-188 turbidimeter (INESA, China). Briefly, the minerals (1 g) were poured into the flotation cell and then the reagent was added. The addition sequence and pulp mixing procedure are the same as that of the micro-flotation tests. After that, the pulp was poured into a cylinder with stopper (100 mL) and was then thoroughly shaking for 3 min. The mixture was allowed to settle under ambient condition for another 3 min. The upper suspension (20 mL) was pumped into the bottle of turbidimeter for measurement. Each test was repeated three times and the average value was taken.

For adsorption tests, the pulp mixture was obtained according to the micro-flotation procedure. After the adsorption of SBX by the mineral, the absorbance of the residual solution was measured by a 752 ultraviolet visible spectrophotometer (Youke Instrument, China) at the wavelength of 300 nm to determine the concentration of SBX. Since the synthesized St-Ba in water is a suspension, its concentration can’t be measured as common solutions. So, the concentration of St-Ba was determined by measuring the turbidity of the suspension. Firstly, a standard curve between turbidity and St-Ba concentration was measured and shown in Fig. 3. The Pearson correlation coefficient (r) is about 0.99915, indicating that the concentration of St-Ba is well linear proportional to the turbidity. The adsorption capacity (Γ) of St-Ba on minerals can also be calculated by Eq. (1).

In order to study the adsorption characteristics of SBX and St-Ba on mineral surface, the infrared spectrum was characterized by using an Infrared spectrometer (Perkin Elmer, USA.). 1 g of mineral (~2 µm) was added into the prepared solutions with the collectors (SBX, 1 × 10−3 mol·L−1; St-Ba, 17.6 g·L−1) and stirred for 10 min. Subsequently, the minerals treated by SBX or St-Ba were then washed with deionized water at the same pH value with the collector solutions. After drying in natural air, the FT-IR of minerals adsorbed with reagent was determined.

The surface morphology of synthesized St-Ba and minerals was observed by SEM (MLA650FFEI, USA). The synthesized St-Ba was diluted by 20 times, and then 1 drop of St-Ba suspension was dropped on copper holder and then observed after freeze-drying.

The SEM image of St-Ba nanospheres adsorbed on mineral surface was also recorded. 0.5 g minerals were added in the diluted St-Ba, stirred for 5 min, and then settled by gravity for 3 min. Pouring out the supernatant and adding 20 mL of deionized water to the deposition mixture. After thoroughly shaking, 1 drop of the mixture was dropped onto the copper support, and then observed after freeze-drying.

For the SEM observation of serpentine depositing on the chalcopyrite surface, 0.1 g serpentine and 1 g chalcopyrite were placed into 100 mL deionized water. After sufficient mixing and pH adjustment, the mixture was filtered and dried for SEM observing.

NX10 atomic force microscope (Park, Korea) was used to observe the morphology and size of the synthesized St-Ba. The diluted St-Ba were dropped on the clean silicon wafer, and then dried with N2 flow. Following the sample was scanned in the ambient air at 20.0 ± 2.0 ℃ and relative humidity of 38.5 ± 5.5% using a Si3N4 probes (OMCL-AC160TS 10 M, Park, Korea) with a nominal force constant of 26 N/m and a resonant frequency of 300 kHz.

ce:section.ce:section-title: MD simulation on the interaction behavior between St-Ba molecule model and chalcopyrite (112) surface
ce:section.ce:para: To reveal the mechanism of St-Ba nanospheres adsorbing on the chalcopyrite (112) surface, MD simulation on the interaction behavior between St-Ba molecule and chalcopyrite (112) surface was performed. The three-dimensional (3D) molecular structures of chalcopyrite and St-Ba used in the simulation process were optimized and generated by material studio 2016 (MS) software ( Fig. 4). Due to the high degree of polymerization of nanospheres, styrene butyl acrylate with five degrees of polymerization was used as the model of St-Ba to facilitate the simulation. In the simulation process, the consistent valence force field (CVFF) was used to describe the interaction potential energy between the chalcopyrite (112) surface and St-Ba in the simulation system, and the charge parameters of all atoms in the simulation system came from CVFF database and remained constant [28]. MD simulation was carried out in large-scale atomic/molecular massively parallel simulator (LAMMPS), and the rectangular box was selected as the periodic boundary condition. The simulation ensemble adopted NVT ensemble under the conditions of pressure 0.1 MPa and temperature 300 K [28,29]. The nonbonding potential energy between atoms was described by the Lennard-Jones potential, with the cut off of 1 nm. The time step was 1fs, atomic trajectories and other thermodynamic data were recorded every 20 ps, and a total of 1000 groups of data were recorded.

The morphological images of the St-Ba nanospheres were characterized by SEM and AFM and shown in Fig. 5. It was shown that various nanoparticles were uniform spherical and the sphere size was in the range of 150–200 nm.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of serpentine on flotation performance of chalcopyrite
ce:section.ce:para: The effect of serpentine on the flotation behavior of chalcopyrite at different pulp pH was studied and shown in Fig. 6(a). It was found that using SBX as collector, chalcopyrite single mineral exhibited a high floatation recovery in the test pH range, and the single serpentine had a very poor floatability. However, the micro-flotation experiment of mixed ore showed that the addition of serpentine significantly reduced the recovery of chalcopyrite. Moreover, the pH value had a great influence on the flotation performance of chalcopyrite in the presence of serpentine. With the increase of pH value from 2 to 10, the recovery of chalcopyrite decreased from 89.08% to 42.41%. The results indicated that serpentine strongly depressed the chalcopyrite flotation, which is consistent with the previous reports [30]. Effect of the serpentine concentration on the floatability of chalcopyrite was further studied. As shown in Fig. 6(b), the flotation recovery of chalcopyrite greatly decreased from 86.74% to 35.55% with the increase of serpentine concentration from 0 to 7.5 g·L−1. When the concentration of serpentine was over 7.5 g·L−1, the recovery of chalcopyrite changed little. Such finding indicates that the serpentine has a serious influence on the floatability of chalcopyrite.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Enhanced collection of chalcopyrite by St-Ba
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 7(a) shows the effect of St-Ba concentration on the floatability of serpentine and chalcopyrite single minerals. It can be seen that chalcopyrite had a high recovery, while serpentine exhibited poor floatability. When the concentration of St-Ba increased to 1.76 g·L−1, the recovery of chalcopyrite reached 93.03% and remained nearly unchanged with the further increase of the St-Ba concentration. In contrast, the serpentine recovery was very poor even under a high concentration of the St-Ba. The effect of St-Ba on the floatability of the two single minerals was further studied under different pH values (Fig. 7b). Obviously, chalcopyrite has good floatability in the whole pH range of 2–12. Especially, the floatation recovery of chalcopyrite will be higher under alkaline conditions. However, serpentine has poor floatability in the whole pH range. These results indicated that St-Ba is an effective collector for chalcopyrite.

Within the pH range of the flotation solution used, chalcopyrite surface is negatively charged and St-Ba surface is positively charged [24,31], so electrostatic attraction will be existed between them. Moreover, both the surfaces of chalcopyrite and St-Ba are hydrophobic [24,32] and hydrophobic attractive force will be occurred between the two particles. Therefore, the St-Ba nanospheres are very easy to adhere to the surface of chalcopyrite through the electrostatic and hydrophobic attraction forces. In contrast, the surface of serpentine is hydrophilic and positively charged. Therefore, it is not only the hydrophobic attraction disappeared but also electrostatic repulsion generated between serpentine and the St-Ba nanospheres, leading to the difficult aggregation of them. As a result, the St-Ba nanospheres has a good effect on the chalcopyrite flotation but not on the serpentine.

As mentioned above, when SBX was used as collector, serpentine has a serious adverse impact on the floatability of chalcopyrite (Fig. 6). To further illustrate whether St-Ba can still enhance the floatability of chalcopyrite in the presence of serpentine, micro-flotation experiments of the artificial mixed ore of chalcopyrite and serpentine were performed. As shown in Fig. 8, St-Ba had an excellent collection capacity for chalcopyrite even in the presence of serpentine. Obviously, compared with the traditional collector SBX used in mineral flotation industry, the St-Ba nanospheres exhibited better collection performance for chalcopyrite. The inhibition of serpentine on the floatability of chalcopyrite was basically eliminated by St-Ba nanospheres.

ce:section.ce:section-title: The enhanced floatability mechanism by St-Ba

ce:section.ce:para: The floatability of mineral greatly depends on the mineral surface wettability. Fig. 9 shows the contact angle measurements of two minerals after SBX and St-Ba nanospheres treatment. It was found that after the mineral surface was treated with SBX or St-Ba nanospheres, the serpentine exhibited a low contact angle of about 40°, while the chalcopyrite shown a relative high contact angle of over 70°. Especially, the chalcopyrite treated by St-Ba nanospheres exhibited a higher contact angle than that treated by the SBX. These results indicate that the St-Ba nanospheres are more contributed to the surface hydrophobicity of chalcopyrite, and thereby improve the floatability of chalcopyrite.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Agglomeration of the chalcopyrite and serpentine mineral particles
ce:section.ce:para: The floatation results in Fig. 6 show that the serpentine has a serious adverse influence on the floatability of chalcopyrite. It is believed that such a result is possibly related to the attachment of the serpentine particles on the chalcopyrite surface. To investigate the aggregation/dispersion of various particles, the turbidity of the mixture solution was tested. The turbidity can reflect the dispersive state of particles in pulp. The more turbid the system is, the better the dispersion of particles will be. On the contrary, a high transparency of the system indicates a strong agglomeration between particles. Fig. 10(a) shows the pulp turbidity of the single and mixed minerals of chalcopyrite and the serpentine at different pH. It is shown that for single mineral system, the turbidity of serpentine is much higher than that of the chalcopyrite, which attributes to the fact that the particle size and density of chalcopyrite is much larger than that of serpentine. The large chalcopyrite particles are deposited to the bottom, while the serpentine fines can be well dispersed in the pulp. Therefore, the pulp turbidity will mainly depend on the concentration and dispersion of serpentine in the pulp. For the chalcopyrite-serpentine system, the turbidity of mixed ores was considerably decreased comparing to that of the single serpentine mineral, indicating that part of the serpentine fines slime-coated on the chalcopyrite surfaces. In addition, the turbidity value of mixed ores gradually decreased with the increase of pulp pH, indicating that the higher the pulp pH value, the more serious the heterogeneous aggregation between serpentine and chalcopyrite.

The effect of serpentine concentration on the pulp turbidity was further studied. As shown in Fig. 10(b), with the increase of the serpentine concentration, the turbidity of both single serpentine and mixed mineral pulps first increased rapidly, and then gradually declined as the serpentine concentration exceeded 4 g·L−1. Such finding indicates that the particle agglomeration occurs not only heterogeneously between serpentine and chalcopyrite, but also homogeneously in the serpentine fines.

FTIR has been widely used to explore the adsorption characteristics of reagents on mineral surface [33]. To reveal the adsorption of St-Ba nanospheres on the surface of chalcopyrite and serpentine, FT-IR spectra of various materials were recorded. As shown in Fig. 11, for the St-Ba nanospheres, the peaks at 2960 cm−1 and 2870 cm−1 are ascribed to the stretching vibration of -CH3, and the peak at 1375 cm−1 is due to the bending vibration of -CH3 [34,35]. The peaks at 2925 cm−1 and 2850 cm−1 are derived from the asymmetric and symmetric stretching vibration of -CH2 [35,36]. The absorption peaks at 3082 cm−1, 3061 cm−1and 3027 cm−1 are corresponding to C-H in aromatic group [34], while the peaks at 1601 cm−1, 1493 cm−1 and 1450 cm−1 are assigned to the stretching vibrations of the aromatic ring skeleton (CC) [35,37]. The peaks at 698 cm−1 and 757 cm−1 are attributed to the bending vibration of monosubstituted benzene ring [36,38]. The peaks at 1260 cm−1 and 1160 cm−1 are mainly attributed to the symmetric stretching vibrations of C-O-C [39,40], and the peak at 1730 cm−1 is related to the stretching vibration of CO [35,38,40].

For the serpentine before treatment by St-Ba nanospheres, peak at 3688 cm−1 and peaks at 611 cm−1 and 441 cm−1 are assigned to the Mg-OH stretching vibration [41] and bending vibration [42], respectively. The peaks at 3440 cm−1 and 1631 cm−1 are derived from the stretching and bending vibration of –OH of the connate water in the mineral [42]. The peaks at 1076 cm−1 and 957 cm−1 are corresponding to the Si-O-Si apical stretching vibration and Si-O-Si basal stretching vibration [43], while the peak at 568 cm−1 is attributed to bending vibration of Si-O. After the serpentine interacting with the St-Ba nanospheres, there is no new peak appeared, indicating that the St-Ba nanospheres were not adsorbed on the serpentine surface. In contrast, for the treated chalcopyrite sample by St-Ba, some typical peaks of the St-Ba material are appeared in the FT-IR spectrum. For instance, the stretching vibration peaks of –CH2 at 2925 cm−1 and 2850 cm−1 and the peak at 1750 cm-1 for the stretching vibration peak of CO. Such finding indicates that St-Ba can be well adsorbed on the chalcopyrite surface, so it is a good collector for recovering the chalcopyrite.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Adsorption behavior of the collectors on mineral surface
ce:section.ce:para: The adsorption of collectors on mineral surfaces is a key step for a successful flotation. The adsorption behavior of SBX on surfaces of chalcopyrite and serpentine was studied. Fig. 12(a) shows the adsorption quantity of SBX on chalcopyrite and serpentine under different SBX concentrations. It can be seen that SBX has almost no adsorption on the surface of serpentine. In contrast, SBX exhibited high adsorption quantity on the surface of chalcopyrite and increased with the increase of SBX concentration. When the SBX concentration was over 1.0 × 10−4 mol·L−1, the adsorption quantity was no longer changed significantly. Fig. 12(b) shows the effect of the serpentine presence on the SBX adsorption on chalcopyrite surface at different pH. It was found that the adsorption quantity of SBX on single chalcopyrite was high at various pH, however, which was greatly decreased in the presence of the serpentine especially at high pH condition. This can be attributed to the slime-coating of serpentine fines on the surface of chalcopyrite, which inhibits the adsorption of SBX. Such a finding is well consistent with the floatation results in Fig. 6.

The adsorption behavior of St-Ba nanospheres on surfaces of chalcopyrite and serpentine was further studied. Fig. 13 shows the effect of St-Ba concentration and pulp pH on the adsorption of St-Ba on the mineral surface. The results showed that the adsorption behavior of St-Ba on the single minerals of chalcopyrite and serpentine was very similar with that of the SBX. That is, the St-Ba nanospheres can be well adsorbed on the surface of chalcopyrite, but not on the surface of serpentine. The difference is that the St-Ba nanospheres still have good adsorption on the surface of mixed ores in the measured pH range, although the adsorption capacity is a little bit lower than that of the single chalcopyrite. Therefore, the heterogeneous aggregation of serpentine with the chalcopyrite has limited effect on the adsorption of St-Ba on the chalcopyrite surface. The above result is well consistent with the micro-flotation results in Fig. 8.

The heterogeneous aggregation of serpentine and chalcopyrite, and the adsorption of the St-Ba on the surface of chalcopyrite were observed by SEM. As shown in Fig. 14, the surface of chalcopyrite is very clean, and the surface elements are mainly composed of sulfur, iron and copper (Fig. 14a). For the mixture of serpentine and chalcopyrite (Fig. 14b1–b2), it is clearly observed that the surface of chalcopyrite was covered by a large number of serpentine fines, and the elements composition increases the oxygen, magnesium and silicon. Such a finding further confirms that serpentine and chalcopyrite are prone to heterogeneous aggregation. The SEM images of the St-Ba nanospheres on chalcopyrite surface are shown in Fig. 14(c1–c2). It can be observed that the St-Ba nanospheres are stably adsorbed on the surface of chalcopyrite, proving that the St-Ba nanoparticle is a good collector to recover the chalcopyrite by flotation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: MD simulation on the interaction behavior of St-Ba molecule with chalcopyrite (112) surface
ce:section.ce:para: The interaction behavior between St-Ba and chalcopyrite (112) surface was studied by MD simulation. The total interaction energy between St-Ba and the chalcopyrite (112) surface was recorded and shown in Fig. 15(a). It was found that with the extension of simulation time, the interaction energy gradually increased and finally stabilized at −1.99 ± 0.50 × 10−18 J. The interaction energy was negative, indicating that the adsorption process was exothermic and spontaneous. Fig. 15(b) shows the snapshots at representative time steps for the St-Ba molecules along the trajectory of the chalcopyrite (112) surface. It was observed that the St-Ba molecule has adhered to the chalcopyrite (112) surface at 2.5 ns, and the whole St-Ba molecular chain gradually spreads on the chalcopyrite (112) surface. The MD simulation indicates that there is a strong interaction between the St-Ba molecule and chalcopyrite (112) surface. Therefore, the St-Ba nanospheres can be easily adsorbed on the surface of chalcopyrite.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Mechanism of the enhanced flotation by St-Ba nanospheres
ce:section.ce:para: Based on the flotation results and various characterizations, the mechanism on the enhanced floatability of chalcopyrite by St-Ba nanospheres was revealed and illustrated in Fig. 16. SBX can well adsorb on the chalcopyrite surface but not on the surface of serpentine (Fig. 12). Theoretically, it is a good collector for the chalcopyrite mineral even in presence of serpentine fines in the pulp. However, it was found that the floatability of chalcopyrite was considerably deteriorated for the artificial mixed ore of chalcopyrite and serpentine. It is believed that such a result is closely related to the slime-coating of the serpentine fines on the chalcopyrite surface (Figs. 10 and 14). Because the size of the serpentine particle is much larger than that of SBX molecule, it is difficulty for the air bubble directly contacting the SBX adsorbed on the surface of chalcopyrite due to the steric hindrance of serpentine (Fig. 16a). As a result, the recovery of chalcopyrite was greatly decreased in the presence of serpentine (Fig. 6). When the St-Ba nanospheres were used as the collector, St-Ba could well adsorb on the surface of chalcopyrite, making the chalcopyrite surface have good hydrophobicity (Fig. 9). Moreover, the St-Ba nanosphere has a larger size than that of the serpentine (Fig. 14), it can be acted as a bridge between chalcopyrite and the air bubbles. Therefore, through the bridging effect of the St-Ba nanospheres, chalcopyrite mineral particles can adhere to the surface of bubbles and be floated (Fig. 16b).

In this work, the synthesized St-Ba nanosphere was applied as a novel collector to enhance the floatability of chalcopyrite inhibited by serpentine. Compared with the conventional collector of SBX, the St-Ba nanospheres enhanced the floatation recovery from 89% to 95% for the single chalcopyrite mineral, and from 42% to 84% for the mixed ores of chalcopyrite and serpentine. The collection mechanism of St-Ba for chalcopyrite in the presence of serpentine was studied and revealed. The major conclusions of this work are as follows:
(1)
Both SBX and the synthesized St-Ba nanospheres can be well adsorbed on the chalcopyrite surface but not on the surface of serpentine. Therefore, they are all good collectors for single chalcopyrite minerals. However, when the SBX was used to process the artificial mixed ores of chalcopyrite and serpentine, the floatability of chalcopyrite was seriously inhibited by serpentine. In contrast, the synthesized St-Ba nanosphere was found to be an effective collector improving the floatability of chalcopyrite in the presence of serpentine.
(2)
It is believed that the inhibition of serpentine on the floatability of chalcopyrite is closely related to the slime-coating of the serpentine fines on the chalcopyrite surface, which hinder the contact of air bubbles with the SBX adsorbed chalcopyrite surfaces. While for the St-Ba nanosphere, it can attach to the surface of chalcopyrite and act as a bridge between chalcopyrite and air bubbles to enhance the floatability of the chalcopyrite minerals.
